teaching.h: Every noun has a gender — and you just have to learn it
teaching.p: This is the single biggest adjustment coming from English: every German noun is masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das), and it's usually NOT related to meaning. A table (der Tisch) is masculine, a bridge (die Brücke) is feminine, a girl (das Mädchen) is grammatically neuter — yes, really. The honest advice every German teacher gives: learn the article together with the noun, as one word, from day one. Don't learn 'Tisch', learn 'der Tisch'.
teaching.ex: der Mann · die Frau · das Kind
teaching.exTranslation: the man (m) · the woman (f) · the child (n)

teaching.h: Definite articles change with gender
teaching.p: 'The' in English is one word. In German it's three, depending on the noun's gender, when that noun is the subject of the sentence.
teaching.ex: Der Mann ist hier.
teaching.exTranslation: The man is here.

teaching.h: Indefinite articles: ein vs. eine
teaching.p: 'A/an' becomes ein for masculine and neuter nouns, and eine for feminine nouns. Notice: there's no plural version of 'ein' — you just drop the article entirely when speaking generally about plural things.
teaching.ex: ein Mann · eine Frau · ein Kind
teaching.exTranslation: a man · a woman · a child

teaching.h: Plurals all share one article
teaching.p: Here's some relief: no matter the original gender, ALL plural nouns use 'die' in the subject position. The tricky part is that the noun itself often changes form to show it's plural — and there's no single reliable rule for how, so plurals also get memorized alongside the singular.
teaching.ex: der Mann → die Männer
teaching.exTranslation: the man → the men

quiz.q: Which article goes with Buch (book, neuter)?
___ Frau ist hier. (the woman is here)
What's the nominative plural article for all genders?
Which indefinite article is correct for a masculine noun?
Das ist ___ Mädchen. (this is a girl)

teaching.h: The pronoun set — smaller than English in one way, bigger in another
teaching.p: German has one word for 'it/he/she' split three ways by gender (er/sie/es), but only ONE word for 'you' that covers singular, plural, formal, and informal is actually split into three: du (one person, informal), ihr (multiple people, informal), and Sie (formal, always capitalized).
teaching.ex: ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie
teaching.exTranslation: I, you (one person, informal), he, she, it, we, you (multiple people, informal), they

teaching.h: Regular verbs: same pattern every time
teaching.p: Take the infinitive, drop the -en, then add an ending that matches the subject. Once you know this one pattern, you can conjugate hundreds of regular verbs correctly.
teaching.ex: machen → ich mache, du machst, er macht, wir machen, ihr macht, sie machen
teaching.exTranslation: to do/make → I do, you do, he does, we do, you all do, they do

teaching.h: sein (to be) — irregular, and you'll use it constantly
teaching.p: Like English 'to be' (am/is/are), German's sein doesn't follow the regular pattern. It's irregular precisely because it's used so often — worth memorizing this one by heart before anything else.
teaching.ex: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind
teaching.exTranslation: I am, you are, he is, we are, you all are, they are

teaching.h: Sie — the formal 'you', always capitalized
teaching.p: When speaking to a stranger, an elder, or in a business setting, use Sie instead of du. It's grammatically treated exactly like 'sie' (they) — same verb endings — but always capitalized to show you mean the formal 'you', not 'they'.
teaching.ex: Sprechen Sie Deutsch?
teaching.exTranslation: Do you speak German? (formal)

quiz.q: Who does du refer to?
Ich ___ Deutsch. (I do/make German — machen)
Er ___ das. (he does that — machen)
What's the correct form of sein for wir (we)?
Which pronoun is the formal 'you'?

teaching.h: What a 'case' actually is
teaching.p: In English, word order tells you who's doing what: 'The dog bites the man' means something different from 'The man bites the dog', even though the words are the same. German instead changes the ARTICLE to show a noun's role in the sentence — this is what 'case' means. It feels foreign at first, but it's what lets German have more flexible word order than English.

teaching.h: Nominative — the one doing the action
teaching.p: This is the 'default' case, the one you already learned in Lesson 1 — used for the subject of the sentence.
teaching.ex: Der Mann sieht den Hund.
teaching.exTranslation: The man sees the dog.

teaching.h: Accusative — the thing receiving the action
teaching.p: Notice in that same sentence: 'den Hund', not 'der Hund'. Only the MASCULINE article changes in the accusative (der→den, ein→einen). Feminine, neuter, and plural articles stay exactly the same as nominative — one less thing to memorize.
teaching.ex: Ich sehe den Mann.
teaching.exTranslation: I see the man.

teaching.h: Dative — the indirect receiver ('to/for whom')
teaching.p: Used for indirect objects, and after certain prepositions like mit (with), bei (at), nach (after/to). This is where all three genders actually change form.
teaching.ex: Ich gebe der Frau das Buch.
teaching.exTranslation: I give the woman the book.

teaching.h: The full article table — the single most useful reference in this course
teaching.p: Here's the full pattern side by side. Bookmark this table — almost every German sentence relies on it, and once it clicks, cases stop being scary.

table.caption: Definite article by case and gender

quiz.q: What does masculine der become in the accusative?
Ich sehe ___ Mann. (I see the man — accusative)
Which case is used for the subject of a sentence?
Ich gebe ___ Frau das Buch. (I give the woman the book — dative)
Do feminine articles change in the accusative case?

teaching.h: The verb-second rule — the backbone of German sentences
teaching.p: In a main clause, the CONJUGATED verb is always the second grammatical element — but 'second' doesn't mean 'second word'. You can start a sentence with almost anything (time, place, an object), and the verb still has to come right after it, which then pushes the subject to third position.
teaching.ex: Heute gehe ich ins Kino.
teaching.exTranslation: Today I'm going to the cinema. (literally: Today go I to-the cinema)

teaching.h: Subordinate clauses flip the rule entirely
teaching.p: After connector words like weil (because), dass (that), or wenn (if/when), the verb jumps all the way to the END of the clause instead. This trips up almost every learner at first — the fix is just repetition until it feels automatic.
teaching.ex: Ich bleibe zuhause, weil ich krank bin.
teaching.exTranslation: I'm staying home because I am sick. (literally: ...because I sick am)

teaching.h: Yes/no questions: verb jumps to first place
teaching.p: To turn a statement into a yes/no question, just move the conjugated verb to the very front — no 'do/does' needed like in English.
teaching.ex: Gehst du ins Kino?
teaching.exTranslation: Are you going to the cinema? (literally: Go you to-the cinema?)

quiz.q: In German main clauses, the conjugated verb is always in position:
Heute ___ ich ins Kino. (today I go to the cinema — gehen)
In a clause starting with weil, where does the verb go?
Ich bleibe zuhause, weil ich krank ___. (...because I am sick — sein)
In a yes/no question, the verb goes:

teaching.h: What modal verbs actually do
teaching.p: können (can), müssen (must), wollen (want to), dürfen (may/allowed to), sollen (should), mögen (like to) — these express ability, necessity, desire, or permission, and they always work together with a second, main verb.

teaching.h: Sentence structure: modal splits from the main verb
teaching.p: The modal verb gets conjugated and sits in position 2, like any verb. But the main verb goes to the very end of the sentence, unconjugated, in its infinitive form. This is the same 'verb-to-the-end' pattern you saw with subordinate clauses.
teaching.ex: Ich kann gut Deutsch sprechen.
teaching.exTranslation: I can speak German well. (literally: I can well German speak.)

teaching.h: können — irregular, and worth memorizing fully
teaching.p: Notice ich and er/sie/es share the exact same form here, with no extra ending — a quirk shared by all modal verbs.
teaching.ex: ich kann, du kannst, er kann, wir können, ihr könnt, sie können
teaching.exTranslation: I can, you can, he can, we can, you all can, they can

teaching.h: The other common modals
teaching.p: müssen = must/have to (a real obligation), wollen = want to (a desire), dürfen = may/am allowed to (permission — the opposite of what it looks like to English speakers who might guess 'dare').

quiz.q: In 'Ich kann gut Deutsch sprechen,' where is sprechen (to speak)?
Ich ___ gut Deutsch sprechen. (I can speak German well — können)
müssen expresses:
Du ___ das nicht machen. (you're not allowed to do that — dürfen)
wollen means:

teaching.h: The word classes — mostly familiar, one big difference
teaching.p: German splits into the same basic categories as English: Nomen (noun), Verb, Adjektiv, Adverb, Pronomen, Präposition, Konjunktion. The one thing that'll instantly change how German text looks to you: nouns.
teaching.ex: laufen (Verb), schnell (Adverb), Lehrer (Nomen)
teaching.exTranslation: to run (verb), quickly (adverb), teacher (noun)

teaching.h: Every single noun is capitalized — always
teaching.p: This isn't a style choice, it's a hard rule. Unlike English, where only proper names get capitals, German capitalizes EVERY noun, mid-sentence or not. Once you notice this, reading German gets much easier — the capital letters are basically pointing at every noun for you.
teaching.ex: Der Tisch ist groß. Ich sehe den Tisch.
teaching.exTranslation: The table is big. I see the table.

teaching.h: Adjectives change their ending to match the noun
teaching.p: When an adjective sits directly before a noun (not after 'is/are'), it takes an ending based on the noun's gender and case. You'll build real intuition for this over the next several lessons — for now, just notice the -e ending here.
teaching.ex: der große Tisch
teaching.exTranslation: the big table

teaching.h: Prepositions and conjunctions do familiar jobs
teaching.p: Präpositionen show relationships in space/time (auf = on, in = in, unter = under). Konjunktionen connect two ideas (und = and, aber = but, weil = because) — you already met weil in the word order lesson.
teaching.ex: Die Katze sitzt auf dem Tisch, aber sie schläft.
teaching.exTranslation: The cat sits on the table, but it's sleeping.

quiz.q: In 'Sie läuft schnell,' what part of speech is 'schnell'?
In German, which word class is always capitalized?
der ___ Tisch (the big table — adjective with ending)
'auf' is an example of a:
'aber' connects two ideas — it is a:

teaching.h: Aussagesatz — the plain statement
teaching.p: A basic declarative sentence. You've been building these since Lesson 1 — verb in position 2, as always.
teaching.ex: Ich gehe nach Hause.
teaching.exTranslation: I'm going home.

teaching.h: Fragesatz — two ways to ask a question
teaching.p: Either flip the verb to the front (yes/no question, which you already know), or lead with a question word (W-Frage) — wer (who), was (what), wo (where), wann (when), warum (why).
teaching.ex: Gehst du nach Hause? Wohin gehst du?
teaching.exTranslation: Are you going home? Where are you going?

teaching.h: Satzreihe — two equal sentences, joined
teaching.p: Connect two complete, independent sentences with und, aber, oder, or denn. The key thing: BOTH halves keep their own normal verb-second order — nothing moves to the end here.
teaching.ex: Ich koche, und du deckst den Tisch.
teaching.exTranslation: I'm cooking, and you're setting the table.

teaching.h: Satzgefüge — a main clause plus a dependent one
teaching.p: This is where the 'verb jumps to the end' rule from Lesson 4 actually gets used in a full sentence. The main clause stays normal; the weil-clause (or dass-, wenn-clause) sends its verb to the end.
teaching.ex: Ich bleibe zuhause, weil es regnet.
teaching.exTranslation: I'm staying home because it's raining.

quiz.q: 'Ich gehe nach Hause.' is an example of a(n):
In a Satzreihe, both clauses keep:
'Ich bleibe zuhause, weil es regnet.' is a:
Ich koche, ___ du deckst den Tisch. (and)
A W-question starts with:

teaching.h: A verb that splits into two pieces
teaching.p: This one genuinely doesn't exist in English, so let's slow down: many German verbs have a prefix that DETACHES and flies to the very end of the sentence in the present tense. The verb 'anrufen' (to call) becomes 'rufe...an' — split across the sentence.
teaching.ex: anrufen → Ich rufe dich an.
teaching.exTranslation: to call → I'm calling you. (literally: I call you [pause]... on/up)

teaching.h: Common prefixes that separate
teaching.p: auf-, an-, ab-, mit-, aus- are the usual suspects. A good habit: whenever you learn a new verb with one of these prefixes, say the full sentence out loud so the split feels natural, not just theoretical.
teaching.ex: aufstehen → Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
teaching.exTranslation: to get up → I get up at seven o'clock.

teaching.h: Inseparable prefixes — these never split
teaching.p: be-, ge-, ver-, ent- are the opposite case: permanently glued to the verb, no matter the sentence. There's no shortcut for knowing which prefix type a new verb has — you learn it alongside the verb itself, same as gender.
teaching.ex: verstehen → Ich verstehe das.
teaching.exTranslation: to understand → I understand that.

teaching.h: In subordinate clauses, the two halves reunite
teaching.p: Remember from Lesson 4: subordinate clauses send the whole verb to the end. When that happens to a separable verb, its two halves rejoin into one word again.
teaching.ex: ..., weil ich dich anrufe.
teaching.exTranslation: ...because I'm calling you.

quiz.q: Ich rufe dich ___. (I'm calling you — anrufen, separated)
Which prefix is typically inseparable?
Ich ___ um sieben Uhr auf. (I get up at seven — aufstehen)
'verstehen' is:

teaching.h: Präsens covers more ground than 'present' does in English
teaching.p: German's present tense is often used for the near future too — no separate 'going to' construction needed most of the time.
teaching.ex: Ich arbeite heute. Ich arbeite morgen.
teaching.exTranslation: I work today. I'm working tomorrow.

teaching.h: Perfekt — the past tense you'll actually hear in conversation
teaching.p: haben or sein (conjugated) + a past participle at the end. Most verbs use haben; verbs of motion or state-change (going, coming, becoming) use sein instead. This is genuinely the most common way Germans talk about the past out loud.
teaching.ex: Ich habe gearbeitet. Ich bin gegangen.
teaching.exTranslation: I have worked. I have gone / I went.

teaching.h: Präteritum — the 'storytelling' past
teaching.p: A single-word past form, much more common in writing (books, news) than speech. One big exception: sein, haben, and the modal verbs DO get used in their Präteritum form even in casual speech — 'ich war' (I was) is far more natural than the Perfekt equivalent.
teaching.ex: Ich arbeitete. Ich war müde.
teaching.exTranslation: I worked. I was tired.

teaching.h: Futur I — for the more distant or emphasized future
teaching.p: werden (conjugated) + infinitive at the end. In casual speech Germans often just use the present tense for the future instead (like Lesson 9's first point) — Futur I adds a bit more certainty or formality.
teaching.ex: Ich werde morgen arbeiten.
teaching.exTranslation: I will work tomorrow.

quiz.q: The most common past tense in spoken German is:
Ich ___ gearbeitet. (I have worked — haben, Perfekt)
Futur I is formed with:
Ich ___ morgen arbeiten. (I will work tomorrow — werden, Futur I)
'Ich war müde' uses which tense?

teaching.h: Real conditions — just present tense doing double duty
teaching.p: For realistic 'if this, then that' situations, German just uses wenn with normal present-tense verbs — no special mood needed, unlike the hypothetical case below.
teaching.ex: Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zuhause.
teaching.exTranslation: If it rains, I'll stay home.

teaching.h: Konjunktiv II — for things that aren't real (yet, or ever)
teaching.p: For hypothetical, unreal, or wishful situations, German switches to a different verb mood. The easiest way to build it: würde (would) + infinitive — this works for almost any verb and is what you'll hear most in real conversation.
teaching.ex: Wenn ich reich wäre, würde ich reisen.
teaching.exTranslation: If I were rich, I would travel.

teaching.h: wäre and hätte — the two irregulars worth memorizing by heart
teaching.p: sein and haben don't use the würde-construction — they have their own short Konjunktiv II forms instead, and you'll hear these constantly.
teaching.ex: ich wäre, ich hätte
teaching.exTranslation: I would be, I would have

teaching.h: Talking about a past that didn't happen
teaching.p: To imagine a different past ('if only I had...'), combine hätte/wäre with a past participle. This is the German equivalent of English's 'would have' constructions.
teaching.ex: Wenn ich Zeit gehabt hätte, wäre ich gekommen.
teaching.exTranslation: If I had had time, I would have come.

quiz.q: 'Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zuhause.' describes:
Wenn ich reich ___, würde ich reisen. (if I were rich — sein, Konjunktiv II)
würde + infinitive is used for:
ich ___ (Konjunktiv II of haben — I would have)
Past hypotheticals use:

teaching.h: Satzglied — a chunk that moves as one unit
teaching.p: A Satzglied is a group of words functioning together as a single sentence element — a subject, an object, a time expression. Recognizing these chunks is what makes German's flexible word order (remember Lesson 4?) actually readable.
teaching.ex: Der alte Mann liest ein Buch.
teaching.exTranslation: The old man is reading a book. ('Der alte Mann' moves as one chunk)

teaching.h: Hauptsatz — a complete sentence on its own
teaching.p: Verb in position 2, can stand entirely alone. You've been writing these since day one.
teaching.ex: Ich lese ein Buch.
teaching.exTranslation: I'm reading a book.

teaching.h: Nebensatz — depends on a Hauptsatz to make sense
teaching.p: This is the formal name for the 'verb goes to the end' pattern you already know from weil-clauses.
teaching.ex: ..., weil ich ein Buch lese.
teaching.exTranslation: ...because I'm reading a book.

teaching.h: Relativsatz — a clause that describes a noun
teaching.p: Uses der/die/das (matching the described noun's gender) as a relative pronoun, adding extra detail — like English 'who/which/that'.
teaching.ex: Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Lehrer.
teaching.exTranslation: The man who is standing there is my teacher.

quiz.q: 'Ich lese ein Buch.' is a:
In a Nebensatz, the verb goes:
Der Mann, ___ dort steht, ist mein Lehrer. (who is standing there — relative pronoun)
A Nebensatz can stand alone as a full sentence:
A Relativsatz gives extra information about a:

teaching.h: Aktiv — the doer is the subject
teaching.p: The default, most direct sentence structure — you've been using this the whole course.
teaching.ex: Der Koch kocht das Essen.
teaching.exTranslation: The chef cooks the food.

teaching.h: Passiv — the receiver becomes the subject
teaching.p: Built with werden (conjugated) + a past participle. The focus shifts from who's doing the action to what's being done to.
teaching.ex: Das Essen wird vom Koch gekocht.
teaching.exTranslation: The food is being cooked by the chef.

teaching.h: When Germans actually reach for Passiv
teaching.p: When the doer is unknown, unimportant, or obvious from context — very common in instructions, news, and formal writing.
teaching.ex: Das Fenster wurde zerbrochen.
teaching.exTranslation: The window was broken. (nobody says by whom)

teaching.h: werden changes, the participle doesn't
teaching.p: Across different tenses, only the helper verb werden conjugates — the past participle stays frozen in its one form.
teaching.ex: wird gekocht (present), wurde gekocht (past)
teaching.exTranslation: is cooked, was cooked

quiz.q: 'Der Koch kocht das Essen.' is:
Das Essen ___ vom Koch gekocht. (is cooked by the chef — werden, present)
Passiv is formed with:
Das Fenster ___ zerbrochen. (was broken — werden, past)
Passiv is often used when:
options: the doer is unknown or unimportant
quiz.answer: the doer is unknown or unimportant

teaching.h: Direkte Rede — the exact words
teaching.p: Just like English quotation marks — repeating precisely what someone said.
teaching.ex: Sie sagte: "Ich bin müde."
teaching.exTranslation: She said: "I am tired."

teaching.h: Indirekte Rede — reporting the idea, formally
teaching.p: In formal/written German, indirect speech uses a special mood called Konjunktiv I, which subtly signals 'this is what someone else said, I'm not vouching for it.'
teaching.ex: Sie sagte, sie sei müde.
teaching.exTranslation: She said (that) she was tired.

teaching.h: Konjunktiv I — mostly a written/news thing
teaching.p: You'll encounter this in newspapers and formal reporting far more than in daily conversation.
teaching.ex: er sei
teaching.exTranslation: he is/was (Konjunktiv I of sein)

teaching.h: What people actually say out loud
teaching.p: In everyday spoken German, most people skip Konjunktiv I entirely and just use dass (that) with a completely normal indicative verb — much easier, and totally acceptable in casual speech.
teaching.ex: Sie sagte, dass sie müde ist.
teaching.exTranslation: She said that she is tired.

quiz.q: 'Sie sagte: 'Ich bin müde.'' is:
Sie sagte, sie ___ müde. (she was tired — Konjunktiv I of sein)
Konjunktiv I is mainly used in:
In everyday speech, indirect speech often uses:
Sie sagte, ___ sie müde ist. (that — dass)

teaching.h: The capitalization rule you now already know
teaching.p: You met this back in Lesson 6, but it's worth repeating: every noun, everywhere in the sentence, gets a capital letter — no exceptions.
teaching.ex: Der Hund spielt mit dem Ball.
teaching.exTranslation: The dog is playing with the ball.

teaching.h: A comma is REQUIRED before dass/weil/wenn
teaching.p: Unlike English, where a comma before 'because' is often optional stylistic choice, German requires it before every subordinate clause connector — it's not optional, it's grammar.
teaching.ex: Ich weiß, dass du müde bist.
teaching.exTranslation: I know that you are tired.

teaching.h: Commas in Satzreihen too
teaching.p: When joining two independent clauses with aber, denn, or sondern, a comma is required (though und and oder are more flexible about it).
teaching.ex: Ich wollte kommen, aber ich war krank.
teaching.exTranslation: I wanted to come, but I was sick.

teaching.h: The formal Sie stays capitalized everywhere
teaching.p: Unlike regular nouns which only get capitalized because they're nouns, Sie (formal you) is capitalized specifically to distinguish it from sie (she/they) — and this holds no matter where it falls in the sentence.
teaching.ex: Wie geht es Ihnen?
teaching.exTranslation: How are you? (formal)

quiz.q: In German, which words are always capitalized?
Is a comma required before a dass-clause?
A comma is required before:
The formal 'Sie' is:
options: only capitalized at the start of a sentence

quiz.q: 'Ich wollte kommen, aber ich war krank' — the comma appears because:
options: it joins two independent clauses with aber
quiz.answer: it joins two independent clauses with aber

teaching.h: Reflexive verbs — actions that loop back to yourself
teaching.p: Some verbs need a reflexive pronoun (mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich) that refers back to the subject — often for feelings or self-directed actions, where English would just say 'I'm happy' without any equivalent extra word.
teaching.ex: Ich freue mich. Er wäscht sich.
teaching.exTranslation: I'm happy (literally: I make myself glad). He washes himself.

teaching.h: The genitive case — showing possession, the formal way
teaching.p: des/der + noun, with an added -s (or -es) on masculine and neuter nouns. In casual speech, Germans increasingly use 'von + dative' instead, but genitive still appears constantly in writing.
teaching.ex: das Auto des Mannes
teaching.exTranslation: the man's car

teaching.h: Two-way prepositions — the case depends on movement vs. location
teaching.p: This is a genuinely clever system once it clicks: prepositions like in, auf, unter take ACCUSATIVE when there's movement into a place, but DATIVE when describing a fixed location. Ask yourself 'is something moving into/onto this place, or just sitting there?'
teaching.ex: Ich gehe in die Küche. Ich bin in der Küche.
teaching.exTranslation: I'm going into the kitchen (movement, accusative). I am in the kitchen (location, dative).

teaching.h: Adjective endings — the last major puzzle piece
teaching.p: The ending on an adjective before a noun depends on THREE things at once: the noun's gender, its case, and whether an article comes before the adjective. This feels like a lot at first, but it becomes automatic with exposure far before you can consciously explain the rule.
teaching.ex: der große Hund, ein großer Hund
teaching.exTranslation: the big dog, a big dog (notice the ending changes: -e vs -er)

quiz.q: Ich freue ___. (I'm happy — reflexive pronoun for ich)
The genitive case is mainly used to show:
'Ich gehe in die Küche' uses which case, and why?
'Ich bin in der Küche' uses which case?
der ___ Hund (the big dog — adjective ending with definite article)

teaching.h: What Konnektoren do for your German
teaching.p: These words are what separate choppy, disconnected sentences from writing/speaking that actually flows — they show HOW ideas relate to each other.
teaching.ex: trotzdem, deshalb, außerdem, zum Beispiel
teaching.exTranslation: nevertheless, therefore, additionally, for example

teaching.h: Signaling contrast
teaching.p: trotzdem (nevertheless) and aber (but) both flag that what follows goes against expectation.
teaching.ex: Sie war müde. Trotzdem arbeitete sie weiter.
teaching.exTranslation: She was tired. Nevertheless, she kept working.

teaching.h: Connecting cause and effect
teaching.p: deshalb and deswegen both mean 'therefore/because of that' — genuinely interchangeable in most contexts.
teaching.ex: Es regnete stark. Deshalb wurde das Spiel abgesagt.
teaching.exTranslation: It rained heavily. Therefore, the game was cancelled.

teaching.h: Adding another point
teaching.p: außerdem (furthermore) and zusätzlich (additionally) both stack another related idea onto what you just said.
teaching.ex: Sie ist klug. Außerdem ist sie sehr fleißig.
teaching.exTranslation: She's smart. Furthermore, she's very hardworking.

quiz.q: Which word signals contrast?
Es regnete stark. ___ wurde das Spiel abgesagt. (therefore)
'außerdem' is used to:
'zum Beispiel' means:
Konnektoren mainly help with:
